text: Every company having net worth of Rs. 500 crore or more, turnover of Rs. 1000 crore or more, or net profit of Rs. 5 crore or more during immediately preceding financial year must constitute a CSR Committee and spend at least 2% of the average net profits made during the three immediately preceding financial years. Failure to transfer unspent CSR funds attracts company penalty of twice the unspent amount or Rs. 1 crore (whichever is less) and officer in default penalty of 1/10th unspent amount or Rs. 2 lakh.

A director of a company shall act in good faith to promote the objects of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole, and in the best interests of the company, its employees, shareholders, community and protection of environment. A director shall exercise duties with reasonable care, skill and diligence and shall not involve in a situation where he has a direct or indirect interest conflicting with the company's interest or achieve undue gain. Penalty for contravention is fine not less than Rs. 1 lakh up to Rs. 5 lakh.

marginal_heading: Application to NCLT for Relief in Cases of Oppression and Mismanagement
text: Any member of a company qualified under Section 244 (holding at least 1/10th of issued share capital or 100 members) may file petition before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) complaining that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest, oppressive to any member, or prejudicial to the interests of the company. NCLT possesses wide powers under Section 242 to regulate company affairs, supersede board, or order buyout of shares.

marginal_heading: Punishment for Corporate Fraud (Cognizable and Non-Bailable)
text: Any person found guilty of fraud involving an amount of at least Rs. 10 lakh or 1% of turnover (whichever is less) shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than 6 months which may extend to 10 years and fine not less than the amount involved in fraud up to three times such amount. Where fraud involves public interest, minimum imprisonment is 3 years. Under Section 212(6), offences under Section 447 are cognizable and non-bailable.

marginal_heading: Initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) by Financial Creditor
text: A financial creditor either by itself or jointly with other financial creditors may file an application before the NCLT for initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against a corporate debtor when a default in payment of debt of at least Rs. 1 crore has occurred. Under Supreme Court ruling in Innoventive Industries and Swiss Ribbons, NCLT is only required to verify existence of default from information utility records or bank statements within 14 days.

marginal_heading: Application for CIRP by Operational Creditor & Section 8 Demand Notice
text: An operational creditor (supplier, contractor, employee) can initiate CIRP after serving a 10-day statutory demand notice under Section 8. If the corporate debtor fails to repay the unpaid operational debt (threshold Rs. 1 crore) or fails to demonstrate a pre-existing dispute (prior to delivery of Section 8 notice), the operational creditor can file under Section 9 before NCLT. If a genuine pre-existing dispute exists (Mobilox Innovations ratio), petition must be dismissed.

marginal_heading: Declaration of Statutory Moratorium during CIRP
text: Upon admission of CIRP application, NCLT declares a statutory moratorium prohibiting: (a) institution of suits or continuation of pending suits or proceedings against corporate debtor in any court of law or tribunal; (b) transferring, encumbering or disposing of corporate debtor's assets; (c) any action under SARFAESI Act to enforce security interest; (d) recovery of property by an owner or lessor where occupied by corporate debtor.

marginal_heading: Interim Measures by Court in Commercial Arbitration
text: A party may before, during arbitral proceedings, or at any time after making of arbitral award but before it is enforced under Section 36, apply to a Commercial Court / High Court for interim measures of protection: preserving goods/funds, securing amount in dispute, detention/inspection of property, interim injunctions or appointment of receiver. If court grants interim relief before arbitral proceedings commence, arbitration must commence within 90 days.

marginal_heading: Appointment of Arbitrators by High Court or Supreme Court
text: Where parties fail to agree on arbitrator appointment within 30 days of request, or agreed procedure fails, an application lies to High Court (for domestic arbitration) or Supreme Court (for international commercial arbitration). Under Section 11(6A) and Perkins Eastman doctrine, unilateral appointment of sole arbitrator by an interested party is void ab initio, and the court will appoint an independent arbitrator.

marginal_heading: Application for Setting Aside Arbitral Award (Patent Illegality & Public Policy)
text: Recourse to court against arbitral award can be made only by an application under Section 34 within 3 months (extendable by 30 days max upon sufficient cause). Grounds: (a) incapacity of party; (b) invalidity of arbitration agreement; (c) lack of proper notice; (d) award deals with dispute not contemplated; (e) conflict with Public Policy of India (fraud, fundamental policy of Indian law, basic notions of justice); (f) patent illegality appearing on the face of the award (for purely domestic awards, Associate Builders ratio).

marginal_heading: Agreement in Restraint of Trade Void (Non-Compete & Employment Restraints)
text: Every agreement by which any one is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind, is to that extent void. Exception: Sale of goodwill permits reasonable territorial restraint. Under Supreme Court precedent (Niranjan Shankar Golikari & Percept D'Mark), negative covenants operating during the term of employment are valid, but post-termination non-compete clauses are completely void and unenforceable under Indian law.

marginal_heading: Compensation for Loss or Damage Caused by Breach of Contract
text: When a contract is broken, the party suffering from breach is entitled to receive compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach. Compensation is not given for any remote and indirect loss or damage. The injured party has a statutory duty to take reasonable steps to mitigate the loss.

marginal_heading: Compensation for Breach of Contract Where Penalty Stipulated (Liquidated Damages)
text: When a contract is broken, if a sum is named in the contract as liquidated damages or penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled to receive reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named. Under Supreme Court landmark rulings in Fateh Chand and Kailash Nath Associates, naming a liquidated damage figure does not entitle automatic recovery; the plaintiff must prove actual loss suffered unless proof of damage is impossible.

marginal_heading: Mandatory Specific Performance of Contracts (Post-2018 Amendment)
text: The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of Section 11, Section 14 and Section 16. Post the Specific Relief (Amendment) Act 2018, specific performance is no longer a discretionary equitable remedy; courts are statutorily mandated to enforce contract performance unless falling squarely within the statutory exceptions of Section 14.

No enterprise or association of enterprises shall enter into any agreement in respect of production, supply, distribution, storage, acquisition or control of goods or provision of services which causes or is likely to cause an Appreciable Adverse Effect on Competition (AAEC) within India. Cartels and bid-rigging agreements are presumed to have AAEC. Competition Commission of India (CCI) possesses power under Section 27 to impose penalties up to 10% of average global turnover.

marginal_heading: Abuse of Dominant Position in Enterprise Markets
text: No enterprise or group shall abuse its dominant position. Abuse includes: (a) directly or indirectly imposing unfair or discriminatory condition/price (including predatory pricing); (b) limiting or restricting production of goods or technical development; (c) indulging in practices resulting in denial of market access; (d) making conclusion of contracts subject to supplementary obligations having no connection with subject matter (tying).
